# Deconvolving Tax Evasion {#sec-deconvolution}

::: {.content-visible when-meta="jmp"}
## Deconvolving tax evasion {#sec-deconvolution}
:::

We can do better, however. The test in @sec-testing detects whether unincorporated firms overreport on average, but not how overreporting is spread across firms. Deconvolution recovers the whole distribution of overreporting by removing the output measurement error from the distribution of the observed residual. 

The distribution matters because it shows whether overreporting in a particular industry is concentrated in a few aggressive firms or spread across most firms. The two patterns respond differently to the tax rate. A firm overreports only if the credit on the first fictitious peso exceeds the marginal cost of evasion; otherwise it reports truthfully (@eq-foc-noeva). Among the firms that overreport, the amount differs because the cost of evasion depends on productivity. The test rejection can therefore arise from many firms that each overreport a little or from a few firms that overreport a lot while the rest report truthfully. When the tax rate changes, a firm that already overreports adjusts the overreporting amount (intensive margin), while a truthful firm starts to overreport only if the rate rises enough for the credit to exceed its marginal cost of evasion (extensive margin). The distribution shows how many firms sit near the truthful corner, where a change in the rate can make them start or stop overreporting.

In the five largest industries where the test rejects at the 1 percent level and the deconvolution applies, unincorporated firms overreport on average between 4.5 and 23.1 percent of their true materials, depending on the industry. Moreover, most firms overreport. In every industry, the 10th percentile of the distribution lies between 3.2 and 18.0 percent of true materials.


::: {.content-hidden when-meta="jmp"}
## The convolution
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="jmp"}
### The convolution
:::

<!-- The observed residual is overreporting blurred by measurement error, and deconvolution removes the blur. Two results from @sec-testing make this possible.  -->

By @asm-independence, measurement error is independent of overreporting and of juridical organization. Its distribution, $f_\varepsilon$, is therefore the same for corporations and unincorporated firms and known from corporations, whose residual is $-\varepsilon_{it}$ (@sec-testing-beta).

Because $\mathcal V_{it}$ is the sum of two independent terms, $u_{it}$ and $-\varepsilon_{it}$, the density of the observed residual among unincorporated firms is the convolution of the densities of overreporting and of measurement error [@Meister2009]:

$$
f_{\mathcal{V}}(\mathcal{V})=\int f_u(\mathcal{V}+\varepsilon)f_{\varepsilon}(\varepsilon)\,\text{d}\varepsilon,
$$ {#eq-conv}

where $f_{\mathcal V}$ and $f_u$ denote the densities of $\mathcal V_{it}$ and $u_{it}$ among unincorporated firms. The data give $f_{\mathcal V}$, corporations give $f_\varepsilon$, and $f_u$ is the only unknown. Deconvolution solves @eq-conv for $f_u$. @sec-app-deconvolution describes the estimator, a spline density fitted by penalized maximum likelihood.

Deconvolution works here because, under Cobb-Douglas, the elasticity is constant: the log ratio of reported to true materials enters the residual as an additive term, and no other term in the residual depends on the firm's materials or other inputs. In this setting, deconvolution is a simple and elegant tool: it needs only reported shares, the corporations' residuals and @eq-conv.

<!-- Already explained: 
The log share of true materials equals $\ln\beta-\varepsilon_{it}$ for every firm, regardless of its true materials or productivity. This holds for firms that overreport as well, because neither the probability of detection nor the cost of evasion depends on true materials (@sec-model): overreporting leaves the materials condition unchanged and only shifts the reported share by $u_{it}$. The residual therefore splits into two independent terms, overreporting and measurement error, and their densities combine by convolution. In this setting, deconvolution is a simple and elegant tool: it needs only reported shares, the corporations' residuals and @eq-conv. -->

Production functions with an elasticity that varies with materials do not rule out recovering overreporting, but they require either far more data for deconvolution or a different method, such as the one in @sec-counterfactual. With an elasticity $G(M_{it},Z_{it})$ that depends on materials and on the other inputs, $Z_{it}=(K_{it},L_{it})$, the residual would be the reported share minus the log elasticity at reported materials. Corporations identify this elasticity because they report true materials. The residual's overreporting term, $\ln[M^*_{it}/(M^*_{it}-e_{it})]-\ln[G(M^*_{it},Z_{it})/G(M^*_{it}-e_{it},Z_{it})]$, would depend on reported materials and the other inputs as well as on overreporting. If measurement error were also independent of the other inputs, deconvolving the residual conditional on $(M^*_{it},Z_{it})$ would recover the density of this term. A density transformation would then give the density of overreporting, provided the term increases with $e_{it}$. Each value of the conditioning inputs, however, would need its own deconvolution, which would demand far more data than the single deconvolution under Cobb-Douglas.

<!-- That difference depends on the unknown true materials, and the residual would no longer split into independent terms. Other functional forms call for other methods, such as the one in @sec-counterfactual, which writes every unobservable as a function of true materials and estimates the model from moment conditions. -->

::: {.content-hidden when-meta="jmp"}
## The overreporting ratio {#sec-deconvolution-ratio}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="jmp"}
### The overreporting ratio {#sec-deconvolution-ratio}
:::

The deconvolution recovers the density of the log ratio $u_{it}$. To read overreporting as a share of true materials, I transform it into the overreporting ratio, $x_{it}\equiv e_{it}/M_{it}=\exp(u_{it})-1$. Because $x_{it}$ is a monotonic, differentiable function of $u_{it}$, its density follows from a density transformation [@Hogg2019, Theorem 1.7.1],

$$
f_{x}(y)= f_u\big(\ln (1+y)\big)\Bigg|\frac{1}{1+y}\Bigg|,\qquad y\ge0.
$$ {#eq-ratio-dens}

@tbl-overreporting-ratio and @fig-overreporting-ratio show the distribution of the overreporting ratio in the five largest industries, by share of output, that meet two conditions: the test rejects at the 1 percent level, and the residual is at least as dispersed among unincorporated firms as among corporations, which the deconvolution requires.[^variance] @sec-app-pf-all reports all nine industries that enter the structural estimation.

[^variance]: Because overreporting and measurement error are independent (@asm-independence), the variance of the residual among unincorporated firms equals the variance of overreporting plus the variance of measurement error. It therefore cannot fall below the corporations' variance, which is the variance of measurement error alone. I treat the condition as failed when fewer than 5 percent of bootstrap replications, which resample plants, give a ratio of variances of at least 1. Beverages (313) fails it: its unincorporated variance is 0.69 times the corporations', and the ratio reaches 1 in only 3.6 percent of replications.

::: {#tbl-overreporting-ratio}
![](/tables/ch05-overreporting-ratio.png)

Distribution of the overreporting ratio $e/M$ by industry, unincorporated firms.
:::

![Deconvolved density of the overreporting ratio $e/M$ by industry, unincorporated firms.](/figures/ch05-overreporting-ratio.png){#fig-overreporting-ratio}

Overreporting is widespread within industries but differs markedly across them. The mean overreporting ratio ranges from 4.5 percent of true materials in Printing and publishing (342) to 23.1 percent in Wearing apparel (322). In every industry the density has a single peak away from zero. Most unincorporated firms overreport, and few report close to truthfully.

The spread differs across industries as well. In Wearing apparel and Non-metallic minerals (369), firms overreport similar shares of their materials. The 10th and 90th percentiles of these industries lie 6 to 10 percentage points apart. Footwear (324) and Textiles (321) have a long right tail. The 90th percentile is about twice the median in Footwear and one and a half times the median in Textiles. The model attributes these differences within an industry to the cost of evasion, which varies with productivity and with an idiosyncratic shock (@sec-model).
